topic: The Mirror World: Planar Graph Duality and Euler’s Formula
target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students interested in discrete mathematics

outline.topic: The Mirror World: Planar Graph Duality and Euler’s Formula
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students interested in discrete mathematics

sections.title: Prerequisites: The Anatomy of a Planar Map
sections.content: Introduce the components of a planar graph (a graph drawn so no edges cross). Define Vertices (V), Edges (E), and Faces (F). Emphasize that the 'outside' area also counts as one infinite face.
sections.example: Visualize a small island with three houses (Vertices) connected by three paths (Edges) forming a triangle. This layout creates two regions: the inside of the triangle and the vast ocean surrounding it (2 Faces).

sections.title: Euler’s Magic Rule: V - E + F = 2
sections.content: Introduce Euler's Characteristic Formula for connected planar graphs. Explain that regardless of the graph's complexity, the relationship between these three elements remains constant.
sections.example: Take a square-shaped garden. Vertices (corners) = 4, Edges (fences) = 4, Faces (the garden bed + the outside world) = 2. Calculation: 4 - 4 + 2 = 2. Now, add a diagonal fence: V=4, E=5, F=3. 4 - 5 + 3 still equals 2!

sections.title: The Concept of Duality: Creating the 'Mirror' Graph
sections.content: Introduce the transformation process to create a Dual Graph (G*). Each Face in the original graph becomes a Vertex in the dual. If two faces share an edge in the original, their corresponding vertices in the dual are connected by an edge.
sections.example: Imagine a group of Frogs living in the faces (ponds) of our graph. To communicate, each Frog in a pond reaches out to a neighbor in an adjacent pond by jumping over the shared fence (Edge). The Frogs are the new Vertices; their jump paths are the new Edges.

sections.title: Mathematical Symmetry: Swapping V and F
sections.content: Explain the beautiful property of duality: The number of faces in the original graph (F) equals the number of vertices in the dual (V*), and the number of vertices in the original (V) equals the number of faces in the dual (F*). Edges (E) stay the same in count (E = E*).
sections.example: A simple Cube graph has V=8, E=12, F=6. Its dual is an Octahedron, which has V*=6, E*=12, F*=8. The numbers simply swap roles, maintaining the Euler balance: 6 - 12 + 8 = 2.

sections.title: Application: The Dual Perspective in Design
sections.content: Demonstrate why duality matters. It allows us to solve complex problems in one 'world' by looking at their simpler mirror version. This is used in road network planning and printed circuit board (PCB) design.
sections.example: An Ant (the primal graph) wants to guard every gate (Edge) between rooms. A Spider (the dual graph) wants to find a path that visits every room (Vertex) exactly once. By solving the Spider's pathing problem on the dual graph, we can optimize the Ant's patrol route in the original map.

storyboard.title: Prerequisites: The Anatomy of a Planar Map
lecture_lines: A planar graph has no crossing edges.
It consists of vertices, edges, and distinct faces.
The area outside also counts as an infinite face.
animations: Fade in a simple planar graph with 4 vertices and 4 edges.
Highlight the vertices in green (#00FF00) and add 'V' labels.
Pulse the edges in cyan (#00FFFF) and add 'E' labels.
Shade the bounded regions in semi-transparent magenta (#FF00FF).
Label the background area as 'Infinite Face (F)'.

storyboard.title: Euler’s Magic Rule: V - E + F = 2
lecture_lines: Euler’s formula connects vertices, edges, and faces.
For connected planar graphs, V minus E plus F is two.
A square has four vertices, four edges, two faces.
Add a diagonal edge; one face splits into two.
The formula stays: four minus five plus three is two.
animations: Write V - E + F = 2 in bold white (#FFFFFF) text.
Show a square graph with 4 green (#00FF00) vertices and 4 cyan (#00FFFF) edges.
Highlight the interior and exterior faces (F=2) in magenta (#FF00FF).
Display the calculation 4 - 4 + 2 = 2 below the graph.
Add one edge and update formula to 4 - 5 + 3 = 2.

storyboard.title: The Concept of Duality: Creating the 'Mirror' Graph
lecture_lines: Every planar graph has a hidden mirror dual.
Place a new vertex inside every original face.
Connect dual vertices if their faces share an edge.
Each primal edge is crossed by one dual edge.
The dual graph reveals the map's connectivity.
animations: Draw a gray (#808080) triangle graph with one vertex inside.
Place yellow (#FFFF00) dots in the centers of all faces.
Emphasize the dot in the infinite exterior face.
Connect yellow dots with orange (#FFA500) lines crossing primal edges.
Fade the gray graph to focus on the orange dual.

storyboard.title: Mathematical Symmetry: Swapping V and F
lecture_lines: Duality creates a perfect mathematical symmetry.
Faces become dual vertices; vertices become dual faces.
The edge count remains identical for both graphs.
A cube’s eight vertices become an octahedron’s eight faces.
Both graphs maintain the same Euler characteristic.
animations: Display V=8, E=12, F=6 for a primal cube graph.
Animate the numbers swapping to V*=6, E*=12, F*=8.
Show that E=12 remains unchanged in the dual graph.

storyboard.title: Application: The Dual Perspective in Design
lecture_lines: Duality simplifies complex network and circuit designs.
Solving dual problems provides original solutions.
Mirror graphs reveal hidden paths in our physical world.
animations: Show a complex building blueprint as a primal graph.
Draw the dual graph representing movement between rooms.
Transform the dual graph into a sleek circuit board design.
